title: For banks, a breach is now a matter of when, not if, says OCBC’s tech head—and reaction time matters as much as prevention
summary: For banks, trust may now come not from preventing any and all attacks, but from detecting, closing and repairing them faster.
content: Since September, South Korea’s financial sector has been hit by a rolling wave of cyberattacks , with regulators counting 40 incidents at 37 financial firms, including banks, brokerages, insurers, savings banks and crypto exchanges. Researchers traced the September attacks to Artex, an AI-powered tool that automated the intrusions. “With the velocity that cyberattacks are happening, it is a matter of when rather than if,” Praveen Raina, head of group operations and technology at Singapore’s Oversea-Chinese Banking Corp. (OCBC), tells Fortune . For banks, trust may now come not from preventing any and all attacks, but from detecting, closing and repairing them faster. “I wish I could prevent them—and we’ll try—but what we can control is having the right processes so that we can react quickly to whatever happens,” Raina says. His strategy consists of two elements: cybersecurity and resilience. “We’re leveraging AI for cybersecurity,” he explains. “With agentic AI attacking organizations, humans cannot keep up with it… it’s the nature of the beast. So, we’re building a defensive AI wrapper around the bank to protect it.” His team also regularly conducts red-teaming exercises : structured simulations in which a group acts like a real-world attacker to improve their ability to react in the event of a hack. “We practice a lot among ourselves and with other industry players,” Raina says. “We also have a bug bounty program for white hackers to identify [security] issues in exchange for a reward.” Building in-house Raina joined OCBC in 2008 as its SVP in group operations and technology , after spending the early years of his career as an IT consultant to telcos and enterprise software firms in Canada. (OCBC was founded in 1932; Today, it is Singapore’s second-largest bank, and ranks No. 13 on Fortune ’s Southeast Asia 500 list.) In his first year at OCBC, while spending the holidays away from home, Raina amassed a small team to build an iPhone-native banking app. “The tech team was a lot smaller then,” he says. “We didn’t have a deep expertise in building things, and instead mostly bought [our tech solutions] from vendors and implemented them. As the world changed around us, we made it a point [to develop in-house expertise].” (The final product, launched in 2008, was the first digital banking app debuted by one of Singapore’s three local banks: OCBC, DBS and UOB.) From then on, Raina’s team—which today consists of roughly 600 to 700 employees—started building almost everything in-house. “It gives us better control of things, and we can do more and faster releases,” he explains, adding that failing “over and over again” adds to the joy of creation. In July, OCBC launched its Avatar Banking app , which allows clients round-the-clock access to AI-enabled virtual relationship managers. The entire process from ideation to release took four to six weeks, Raina says. “It was an unplanned pregnancy,” he says. “We just happily stumbled upon the idea, and worked every day to generate ideas to see what we could do [to bring it to life].” The new app was initially launched as a beta version to just fifty customers, but Raina says he’s preparing to onboard all the bank’s private wealth clients onto the platform by the first quarter of 2027. (On the app, users can pick between two virtual wealth managers: a man named Wayne and a woman named Wendy.) “The white glove service is always important, and we are not taking that away,” says Raina, who also heads up the tech division at the Bank of Singapore, OCBC’s private banking subsidiary. “The point is, if I wake up at 3 a.m. and want to look at what’s happening with my portfolio, who do I go to? At that time, even if you call your relationship manager, they will likely not pick up.” The quantum frontier Experts estimate that “Q-Day”, the day quantum computers will be able to crack traditional encryption, will happen around the year 2030 . Raina expects a Y2K-style crunch, with every institution competing for the same vendors at the last minute. OCBC is trying to get ahead by training over 100 quantum-literate staff, and running pilots with universities and ST Engineering. “When we go into our mobile banking app, our phone sends a signal to the OCBC data center, and there’s a handshake happening and a key is exchanged to verify our identity,” Raina explains. “The issue with quantum computing is that it’s so powerful that it can break those keys… so the security layer is gone.” Raina compares quantum technology today to AI in the pre-ChatGPT era. “It’s a theoretical field, which we aren’t experts in, so we partner with universities to get a better understanding of the technology stack,” he says. “We are building [quantum security] for the future; we don’t need it today, but when the technology comes to life on Q-Day, we will be ready.” Ultimately, banking is a trust-based business, and Raina sees it as his role to upkeep the faith that users have in OCBC. “People work and they put their life savings with the organization—there’s no bigger trust than that,” he concludes. “We as an organization have to do our part to ensure that everything is protected.” This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

title: Dua Lipa defined internet cool. In a $44 billion creator economy, her successor may be harder to buy
summary: Brands will spend $44 billion on creators this year, but 73% of 13- to 39-year-olds trust small creators more. Strategists see the obsessive, the ghost and the host rising next
content: Being the internet’s cool girl takes surprising work for someone who’s supposed to make it look effortless. She knows about the hole-in-the-wall restaurant before the line wraps around the block, has a vacation wardrobe worth taking notes on, and somehow finds time to read the book everyone will be talking about in six months. Few have mastered that balancing act as well as Dua Lipa. The Grammy-winning pop star has become as much an inspiration for where to vacation, what to read, and where to eat as for what to listen to. She interviews authors like Margaret Atwood for her book club, shares cultural recommendations through her lifestyle platform, Service95, and is a fixture in the fashion world. But after years of celebrities turning their personalities into businesses and influencers making nearly every aspect of their lives shoppable, the economics of being cool may be changing. Being everywhere may no longer make someone worth following, which poses a slight problem for an industry that makes money off visibility. U.S. spending on creator advertising is expected to reach $44 billion this year, more than triple the $13.9 billion spent in 2021, according to the Interactive Advertising Bureau . But even as brands pour more money into the creator economy , younger consumers are growing weary of its biggest stars. A July survey of 13- to 39-year-olds from youth research firm YPulse found that 62% are tired of seeing the same big names everywhere, while 73% trust smaller creators more than big influencers. “You can pay for attention, but you can’t buy cultural credibility or this idea of being cool,” Izzy Farmiloe, global head of strategy and growth at Dazed Studio, the agency arm of youth culture and fashion publisher Dazed Media, told Fortune . How the feed made Dua Lipa Long before Instagram gave celebrities a place to document their breakfast, much of the fascination with the cool girl came from how little the public knew about her. In a November essay for his newsletter, Considered Chaos , brand strategist Eugene Healey explained how each generation’s cool girl was shaped by the media of her time. Kate Moss had fashion magazines, the Olsen twins had the paparazzi, and Alexa Chung had fashion blogs and street-style photographers. Social media brought audiences closer to the women they admired, making relatability an asset for personalities like Emma Chamberlain. As algorithms began serving up content based on people’s interests rather than simply who they followed, celebrities also had more reason to venture beyond the industries that made them famous. “Dua Lipa was made for the feed,” Healey wrote. Her friendship with designer Simon Porte Jacquemus might draw in fashion enthusiasts, while her book club could introduce her to someone who has never listened to Future Nostalgia . Each new audience offers another opportunity to make money beyond selling records and concert tickets. It’s a business model that has become increasingly familiar, with celebrities launching beauty brands, starting newsletters, and inviting followers into their kitchens. Somewhere along the way, having a favorite lip gloss became an opportunity to launch a cosmetics company. Why trying too hard turned uncool The trouble with making a living off being cool is that the more people see someone being paid to recommend things, the harder it becomes to tell what she actually likes. Even the seemingly casual Instagram photo dump, filled with blurry pictures and half-eaten meals, can be as carefully curated as the polished posts it was meant to replace. For Jenna Drenten, a marketing professor at Loyola University Chicago, the problem lies in the very nature of an influencer’s job. “They are expected to sell what is popular, but also expected to discover what’s new,” Drenten told Fortune . Drenten pointed to BookTok, where recommending a novel outside the usual bestseller rotation can set a creator apart. If enough people take her advice, however, the book becomes just another BookTok sensation, losing some of the very appeal that made it worth recommending in the first place. Brands risk falling into the same trap. Farmiloe has seen companies chase the same trends and hire the same talent in their pursuit of relevance, spending money only to end up looking more like one another. “I actually think silence can often be a stronger strategy now,” Farmiloe said. Trying too hard to look polished may also backfire for brands, especially as artificial intelligence makes it easier to produce everything from flawless images to cultural recommendations. “To sort of show mistakes is a way of proving that a human has made something,” Farmiloe said, adding that even typos have become chic. Why the next cool girl may be harder to sell Healey identified three potential successors to the Dua Lipa era: the obsessive, who knows a particular subject inside and out; the ghost, whose reputation spreads without constantly posting; and the host, who brings people together in real life. He argued that the three share expertise and charisma that are hard to fake at a moment when faking has never been easier. If the next dominant medium is an AI model that can summarize the world’s knowledge on demand, Healey wrote, cool becomes whatever can’t be summarized. For brands accustomed to measuring influence in followers, likes, and views, the next cool girl may be much harder to price. Drenten sees growing appeal in people who can offer something beyond a product recommendation, whether it’s a longtime librarian who can introduce readers to literature they might never have discovered on their own or someone who brings strangers together outside the confines of their carefully curated feeds. As going out becomes increasingly expensive, Farmiloe sees an opportunity for brands to help create those experiences. She pointed to Reference Point, a London library, bookshop, and bar that doubles as a gathering place for chess, poetry, and jazz. Rather than paying someone to talk about a brand, companies could give people a place to spend time together. “Instead of just getting noticed, how do you get people to care or actually like engage or spend time with your brand?” Farmiloe said. This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

title: A study of 22,894 Oura Ring wearers ties erratic sleep times to depression and anxiety. Its author offers a simple solution
summary: UCSF and UC San Diego researchers analyzed an average of 154 days of Oura Ring data per person. Lower sleep-regularity scores tracked with worse depression, anxiety, and loneliness.
content: How long you sleep is only part of the picture. In a study of 22,894 adults who wore Oura smart rings for an average of 154 days, people whose bedtimes and wake times shifted from day to day reported more severe depression, anxiety, and loneliness, and the link held after researchers accounted for how long people slept. The research, led by UC San Francisco and UC San Diego and published Nov. 12 in Scientific Reports , measured consistency with the Sleep Regularity Index (SRI) , a 0-to-100 score. A score of 100 means someone falls asleep and wakes up at identical times every day; lower scores mean more drift. Sleep trouble is common. In 2020, 14.5% of U.S. adults had trouble falling asleep most days or every day, and 17.8% had trouble staying asleep, according to the CDC. Most advice for them centers on duration and habits, from the best sleeping position to a consistent bedtime routine . The findings also come as sleep tracking turns into big business. Oura, whose rings supplied the data and which helped fund the study, put its planned IPO on hold this fall ; at the top of its proposed range, the offering would have valued the company at $15.6 billion. Why months of data beat a single week Participants took part in TemPredict, a study launched in 2020 that used smart-ring sleep and movement data synced to the Oura app. They also completed monthly surveys on depression, anxiety, and loneliness. Researchers compared the full multi-month record against a seven-day “Typical Week” snapshot, the window most earlier sleep-regularity studies relied on. Both approaches pointed the same way, but the longer data showed stronger links to mental health. An irregular sleeper’s single week might happen to catch an unusually steady stretch. “We capture the ups and the downs, the harder weeks and the easier weeks, and we obtain a more complete picture of what someone’s sleep looks like over time,” said Ashley Mason, the study’s senior author and an associate professor of psychiatry and behavioral sciences at UCSF. “Short-term tracking may underestimate—but may overestimate—irregular sleep, depending on when you capture it.” Longer tracking, Mason said, can “minimize the impact that unrepresentative weeks have on a dataset.” She pointed to a UK Biobank analysis of nearly 80,000 participants that relied on one week of wrist-worn sleep data. Shyamal Patel, Oura’s senior vice president of science, said the signal from longer tracking was stronger than in a “typical week” snapshot, “which is how much shorter past studies measured sleep regularity. That’s exactly how Oura can support researchers–by making sleep-wake patterns measurable in everyday life over time, especially when paired with repeated assessments of mood and symptoms. Then, randomized interventions can test whether changing sleep routines changes outcomes.” What the numbers show According to first author Severine Soltani, an SRI of 84 corresponds to going to bed and waking up roughly an hour earlier or later than the day before, on average. At 75, that shift is closer to an hour and a half. Scores tracked symptom severity. Participants with severe depression averaged an SRI of 74.93, compared with 83.74 for those within normal limits. For severe anxiety, the average was 78.94, versus 83.67. Each 5-point drop in SRI was associated with roughly 1.5 times higher odds of severe depression. That association held after the researchers adjusted for age, sex, and average sleep duration. Mason calls the findings “correlational in nature.” She pointed to a JAMA Psychiatry study published in February, which found that irregular sleep predicted depressive relapse among adults in remission, as evidence that prioritizing regular sleep may lower the risk of declining mental health. “Sleep irregularity most likely harms mental health through circadian misalignment and its downstream effects—on hormones, inflammation, neurotransmitters, emotion regulation, and our social lives,” Mason said. “When we support circadian rhythms, we support other bodily functions.” The loneliness link Participants who reported elevated loneliness averaged an SRI of 81.79, compared with 83.75 for those within normal limits. The authors noted that sleep-regularity research has paid little attention to loneliness, despite its toll on mental health. Mason said her team approached loneliness with an “exploratory mindset” because the connection “hasn’t been studied before.” The result made sense to her once she thought about everyday routines. “If you have a morning workout class that you always go to and see friends at, you are more likely to have a regular time you wake up in order to get to the class,” she said. “Sleep regularity may be associated with other types of schedule regularity that involve social interactions.” Who funded the study, and what it can’t prove The analysis is cross-sectional, and symptoms were self-reported, so it can’t show that irregular sleep causes depression or the reverse. The study notes that participants were disproportionately white, middle-aged, and living in North America and Europe. Because the study began during the COVID-19 pandemic, the researchers focused on main sleep episodes, excluded shift workers, and did not control for factors such as living alone or individual chronotypes. Funding came from the U.S. Department of Defense, the #StartSmall Foundation, and Oura Health Oy. Mason has been paid for consulting work for Oura, and co-author Benjamin Smarr of UC San Diego has been paid for consulting work and holds a financial interest in the company. What to do with it Asked whether Oura plans to turn SRI into real-time guidance, Patel pointed to features the company already offers: Bedtime Guidance and Chronotype , “which together evaluate a user’s circadian rhythm, and provide a personalized bedtime window that appears an hour before it begins.” A Body Clock graph compares members’ recent sleep with their optimal window. Patel said Oura focuses on “giving members perspective rather than fueling fixation.” “We don’t think perfect sleep is the goal. A consistent routine that fits someone’s life is more realistic and easier to keep up,” he said. “We want members to understand their bodies with more confidence, so they can live their fullest and most vibrant life, not spend their time chasing scores.” Mason’s advice requires no device. “We cannot wave a magic wand and make ourselves fall asleep at the same time every day, but we can set an alarm clock and make ourselves wake up at the same time every day,” she said. “If you wake up at the same time every day that ends in D-A-Y (Monday, Saturday, Sunday, Tuesday, and so on), you will start to get sleepy at the same time each night, and your bedtime will regularize.” This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

title: Kevin O’Leary told Gen Z to invest 15% of each paycheck. One worker asked why investors get the profits
summary: In a Jubilee debate, a software engineer pressed the Shark Tank investor on equity at Starbucks and Amazon.
content: Shark Tank investor Kevin O’Leary rehashed a familiar pitch for Americans who want to get rich: spend less, save 15% of every paycheck, and let the gains compound in the stock market. But when O’Leary faced down 20 Gen Z workers in a Jubilee Media-hosted debate, one participant challenged the traditional bargain between labor and capital. Why should employees spend their lives drawing wages while investors get rich off the surplus value they create? “Why should all the money we make doing our work, our labor, why should it go to people like you? We did the work,” the participant, a software engineer named Joe, said to O’Leary. The episode of Jubilee’s YouTube series “Surrounded,” titled “1 Millionaire Boss vs 20 Gen Z Workers,” posted Nov. 15 and put the multimillionaire investor face-to-face with younger workers questioning the rules of the modern economy. The 8-minute exchange over whether workers deserve a bigger piece of the profits they help generate became one of the flashpoints of the nearly two-hour debate. The argument lands as employee ownership gets a mainstream hearing. SpaceX’s June IPO was expected to make more than 4,400 current and former employees millionaires, welders among them . And Mark Cuban has proposed that companies choose between giving every employee stock and paying higher corporate taxes . From Starbucks dividends to Amazon stock grants Joe opened with a Starbucks hypothetical: Why shouldn’t some of the chain’s billions in profits go to the workers making and serving the coffee? O’Leary argued that would shortchange investors who supplied the capital. Joe wasn’t suggesting workers get all the profits, just a bigger share. He pointed to Starbucks’ dividend payments to shareholders as evidence that the company already distributes its profits. Starbucks, which reported $37.9 billion in revenue for the fiscal year that ended Sept. 27, recently raised its dividend. The debate then moved from coffee shops to one of the country’s biggest employers: Amazon, which this year unseated Walmart as No. 1 on the 2026 Fortune 500 . Joe argued that the company offers one of the starkest examples of how pay can split by role. A software engineer with the same ability to execute and work hard as a warehouse employee could potentially receive substantial restricted stock units, or RSUs, as part of their compensation. The warehouse worker, meanwhile, might receive no equity stake, despite long shifts doing physically arduous work. Why, Joe wanted to know, should one employee have a chance to build wealth through company stock while another is limited to a paycheck? O’Leary said the labor market ultimately shapes compensation. If Amazon couldn’t find enough people willing to work in its warehouses, he said, the company would have to increase compensation to attract them. He also questioned whether equity could realistically be distributed across every type of business. “You can’t do that in every business. You can’t give equity to a utility,” O’Leary said. Joe said equity wasn’t the only answer. Companies could also offer dividends or profit-sharing arrangements that give employees a direct financial stake in their success. He pointed to O’Leary’s fellow Shark Tank investor, Mark Cuban, who gave employees equity at companies he founded and has urged every CEO to do the same. If investors can benefit financially when a business grows or is sold, Joe argued, employees who helped create that value should have a chance to benefit, too. The two did find one patch of common ground: SpaceX, where rank-and-file employees became millionaires when the company’s shares took off. O’Leary said he was perfectly fine with that outcome. Joe’s point, however, was that such windfalls are the exception, not the norm. The economy, as structured, funnels the gains from workers’ labor upward while asking employees to build wealth out of whatever is left of their paychecks. What investors bring to the table O’Leary wasn’t particularly receptive to the idea that investors were simply getting rich off other people’s labor. “I worked pretty damn hard to get rich. Really hard,” he said. Joe said that while O’Leary may have worked hard to build his fortune, he questioned what investors contribute beyond their money. O’Leary explained that he looks for entrepreneurs with promising ideas and business plans, then puts his own capital behind them. When Joe asked what he brought to the table, O’Leary answered bluntly. “Money.” The 15% rule meets the rent The exchange eventually circled back to O’Leary’s familiar advice about personal financial discipline. Rather than waiting for companies to distribute profits, he suggested workers take 15% of their weekly earnings and invest it in the stock market. O’Leary has repeatedly offered this advice to younger Americans. The investor has argued that someone earning $68,000 a year could retire a millionaire by consistently investing 15% of their income over a career. But Joe questioned how realistic that prescription was for people already struggling to cover everyday expenses. Earlier in the episode, another participant, a security guard named Kieran, described working 80 hours a week only to spend 55% of his income on rent. O’Leary said people could cut unnecessary purchases from their budgets. Joe pushed back, joking that O’Leary wouldn’t find much to criticize in his own winnowed-down wardrobe. The exchange ended on an unexpected note of encouragement. Apparently impressed by the passion of Joe’s argument, O’Leary told him he’d make “good television” and invited him to come on Shark Tank. Joe declined. “I never will,” he said. “I don’t want to be an entrepreneur, bro. I just want to live.” For a generation staring down rent, gas prices and student loans, that may be the more radical ask. This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

summary: In a Jubilee debate, a software engineer pressed the Shark Tank investor on equity at Starbucks and Amazon.
content: Shark Tank investor Kevin O’Leary rehashed a familiar pitch for Americans who want to get rich: spend less, save 15% of every paycheck, and let the gains compound in the stock market. But when O’Leary faced down 20 Gen Z workers in a Jubilee Media-hosted debate, one participant challenged the traditional bargain between labor and capital. Why should employees spend their lives drawing wages while investors get rich off the surplus value they create? “Why should all the money we make doing our work, our labor, why should it go to people like you? We did the work,” the participant, a software engineer named Joe, said to O’Leary. The episode of Jubilee’s YouTube series “Surrounded,” titled “1 Millionaire Boss vs 20 Gen Z Workers,” posted Nov. 15 and put the multimillionaire investor face-to-face with younger workers questioning the rules of the modern economy. The 8-minute exchange over whether workers deserve a bigger piece of the profits they help generate became one of the flashpoints of the nearly two-hour debate. The argument lands as employee ownership gets a mainstream hearing. SpaceX’s June IPO was expected to make more than 4,400 current and former employees millionaires, welders among them . And Mark Cuban has proposed that companies choose between giving every employee stock and paying higher corporate taxes . From Starbucks dividends to Amazon stock grants Joe opened with a Starbucks hypothetical: Why shouldn’t some of the chain’s billions in profits go to the workers making and serving the coffee? O’Leary argued that would shortchange investors who supplied the capital. Joe wasn’t suggesting workers get all the profits, just a bigger share. He pointed to Starbucks’ dividend payments to shareholders as evidence that the company already distributes its profits. Starbucks, which reported $37.9 billion in revenue for the fiscal year that ended Sept. 27, recently raised its dividend. The debate then moved from coffee shops to one of the country’s biggest employers: Amazon, which this year unseated Walmart as No. 1 on the 2026 Fortune 500 . Joe argued that the company offers one of the starkest examples of how pay can split by role. A software engineer with the same ability to execute and work hard as a warehouse employee could potentially receive substantial restricted stock units, or RSUs, as part of their compensation. The warehouse worker, meanwhile, might receive no equity stake, despite long shifts doing physically arduous work. Why, Joe wanted to know, should one employee have a chance to build wealth through company stock while another is limited to a paycheck? O’Leary said the labor market ultimately shapes compensation. If Amazon couldn’t find enough people willing to work in its warehouses, he said, the company would have to increase compensation to attract them. He also questioned whether equity could realistically be distributed across every type of business. “You can’t do that in every business. You can’t give equity to a utility,” O’Leary said. Joe said equity wasn’t the only answer. Companies could also offer dividends or profit-sharing arrangements that give employees a direct financial stake in their success. He pointed to O’Leary’s fellow Shark Tank investor, Mark Cuban, who gave employees equity at companies he founded and has urged every CEO to do the same. If investors can benefit financially when a business grows or is sold, Joe argued, employees who helped create that value should have a chance to benefit, too. The two did find one patch of common ground: SpaceX, where rank-and-file employees became millionaires when the company’s shares took off. O’Leary said he was perfectly fine with that outcome. Joe’s point, however, was that such windfalls are the exception, not the norm. The economy, as structured, funnels the gains from workers’ labor upward while asking employees to build wealth out of whatever is left of their paychecks. What investors bring to the table O’Leary wasn’t particularly receptive to the idea that investors were simply getting rich off other people’s labor. “I worked pretty damn hard to get rich. Really hard,” he said. Joe said that while O’Leary may have worked hard to build his fortune, he questioned what investors contribute beyond their money. O’Leary explained that he looks for entrepreneurs with promising ideas and business plans, then puts his own capital behind them. When Joe asked what he brought to the table, O’Leary answered bluntly. “Money.” The 15% rule meets the rent The exchange eventually circled back to O’Leary’s familiar advice about personal financial discipline. Rather than waiting for companies to distribute profits, he suggested workers take 15% of their weekly earnings and invest it in the stock market. O’Leary has repeatedly offered this advice to younger Americans. The investor has argued that someone earning $68,000 a year could retire a millionaire by consistently investing 15% of their income over a career. But Joe questioned how realistic that prescription was for people already struggling to cover everyday expenses. Earlier in the episode, another participant, a security guard named Kieran, described working 80 hours a week only to spend 55% of his income on rent. O’Leary said people could cut unnecessary purchases from their budgets. Joe pushed back, joking that O’Leary wouldn’t find much to criticize in his own winnowed-down wardrobe. The exchange ended on an unexpected note of encouragement. Apparently impressed by the passion of Joe’s argument, O’Leary told him he’d make “good television” and invited him to come on Shark Tank. Joe declined. “I never will,” he said. “I don’t want to be an entrepreneur, bro. I just want to live.” For a generation staring down rent, gas prices and student loans, that may be the more radical ask. This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

title: ‘They’ll all go to Florida’: New IRS data reignites the fight over Massachusetts’ millionaires tax
summary: Filers earning $200,000 or more drove 64% of the income loss, per the Pioneer Institute. The 4% surtax still brought in a record $3.38 billion in fiscal 2026.
content: New IRS figures may offer the clearest picture yet of how Massachusetts’ surtax on high-income residents is shaping the state’s population—and the tax base the ballot measure sought to tap. Massachusetts lost a net 31,384 residents to other states and countries between 2023 and 2024, according to IRS data reported by Boston.com . Those departing households took $3.64 billion in adjusted gross income with them. The net migration loss was slightly larger than the year before, though the income loss shrank from $4.18 billion. The numbers arrive nearly four years after the so-called “millionaires tax”—a 4% surcharge on annual income above roughly $1.1 million, indexed to inflation—took effect to fund schools and transportation. The figures capture moves, not their motives . Still, they are fuel for a perpetual debate: Do taxes on high earners drive wealthy households away, undermining the revenue they were meant to raise? New Hampshire and Florida absorb the biggest share Departing residents have clear destinations. New Hampshire gained a net 7,818 residents from Massachusetts, while Florida picked up 6,032. Together, those two states accounted for roughly 44% of Massachusetts’ net migration loss. The money followed the same routes. Massachusetts lost a net $1.29 billion in adjusted gross income to Florida and $869 million to New Hampshire, together about 59% of the state’s total. Neither destination has a state income tax. Each of Massachusetts’ New England neighbors—New Hampshire, Maine, Rhode Island, Connecticut, and Vermont—also gained more residents from the Bay State than it sent back. Young professionals and high earners drove much of the loss, according to an analysis of the IRS data by the Pioneer Institute, a Boston-based think tank. Tax filers ages 26 to 34 made up 43% of the state’s net loss of filers in 2024, and those earning $200,000 or more accounted for $2.32 billion, or 64%, of the net income loss. The IRS tracks migration by comparing addresses on consecutive years’ tax returns, capturing both the number of people on those returns and their adjusted gross income. The traffic ran both ways. New York sent the most newcomers to Massachusetts (13,394), followed by Florida (11,728) and California (8,728). Massachusetts also led its exchanges with a handful of states, with a net gain of 855 residents from New Jersey, plus smaller gains from Louisiana and Indiana. The surtax keeps beating its forecasts Whatever the migration data show, the tax itself has not come up short. The Massachusetts Department of Revenue preliminarily certified $3.38 billion in surtax collections for fiscal 2026 , a record, and well above the $2.4 billion the state budget had assumed . That compares with roughly $3 billion in fiscal 2025 and the $1.8 billion the state reported in May 2024, double what officials expected . Supporters and critics read the same numbers differently. After the IRS’s March release, MassBudget, a Boston-based research group, argued the data showed affordability, not taxes, driving the state’s out-migration . Other states are moving in Massachusetts’ direction regardless. Washington voters on Nov. 3 kept a new 9.9% tax on income above $1 million, and two of the neighbors now gaining Bay Staters, Maine and Rhode Island, enacted their own surcharges on millionaire income this year . An income tax is not a wealth tax The Massachusetts data lands amid a broader debate over whether governments can tax high earners and wealthy households without prompting them to move. But the policies under scrutiny aren’t all the same. Massachusetts’ millionaires tax is an income tax surcharge: It adds 4 percentage points to the state income tax on annual income above the threshold. California’s Proposition 40, which voters rejected on Nov. 3, targeted wealth itself, with a one-time 5% tax on the net worth of the state’s roughly 200 billionaires. A wealth tax can apply even when assets are “unrealized,” meaning they haven’t been sold or generated taxable income. Peter Barnes, a former U.S. deputy international tax counsel and longtime General Electric tax lawyer, said the history of wealth taxes abroad warns states attempting them on their own. He noted that France saw flight from its wealth tax and has since effectively eliminated it, replacing it in 2018 with a narrower levy on real estate. “That’s the same thing that doomed the California wealth tax—this idea that, ‘Oh my god, they’ll all go to Florida,’” Barnes said. “I think first of all, it needs to be a whole U.S. federal tax. I don’t think a state can successfully do it.” Chester Spatt, a professor of finance at Carnegie Mellon University, previously told Fortune he was skeptical that steep wealth taxes can generate the revenue their proponents expect. “It would indirectly represent a very heavy tax on investment income,” Spatt said. “I suspect it won’t raise much revenue and instead lead to the development of devices that would be outside the reach of the tax.” For now, Massachusetts remains a laboratory of democracy—testing whether taxing high earners at the state level can work, or whether, as critics warn, it simply accelerates their departure. title: Black and Latino workers are about 20% likelier than White workers to need a new career by 2035 as AI reshapes work, McKinsey says
summary: McKinsey projects AI could eliminate more of the work in jobs Black and Latino workers hold, and fewer have a clear path out.
content: Black and Latino workers are about 20% more likely than White workers to need to move into an entirely new occupation by 2035 as AI and automation reshape work, according to projections in a new report from the McKinsey Institute for Economic Mobility released Nov. 20. AI and automation could take over about the same share of work across racial groups, McKinsey projects. What differs is whether that work disappears. McKinsey estimates that automation could reduce an average of 21% of current U.S. work hours by 2035. Of the hours it takes over, 40% of those worked by Black workers and 41% of those worked by Latino workers would be displaced, compared with 37% for White workers and 36% for Asian workers, meaning employers would need fewer people, rather than an augmented environment in which the technology supports a person doing the job. The report ties the gap to the kinds of jobs people hold. Automation is most likely to replace tasks that are standardized, easy to check and low-stakes when wrong. McKinsey’s example is answering a routine billing question, as opposed to adjusting a patient’s medication dose. Tasks like the billing question make up a larger share of the hours Black and Latino workers put in. Physical work, which is increasingly exposed to robotics, accounts for 35% of Black workers’ hours and 39% of Latino workers’ hours, compared with 26% for White workers. The jobs most exposed to AI are predominantly held by Black and Latino workers. McKinsey Report “Our research indicates that while AI and automation are expected to affect a similar share of work hours across racial groups, the consequences may differ significantly,” Duwain Pinder, a partner at McKinsey & Company, said to Fortune in a statement. “While displacement doesn’t vary significantly between cognitive and physical work, the central question is not only how much work AI and automation technologies can perform, but whose work it replaces and through which types of activities.” The effects are projected to concentrate in specific jobs: Black workers hold more than their share of the workforce in each of the six occupations with the steepest projected declines in labor demand. Latino workers hold 43% of hand packer and packager jobs, 2.3 times their share of the workforce. The differences carry into projected job growth. Based on today’s jobs, McKinsey projects total work hours for Latino workers will grow 1.4% between 2025 and 2035 and 2.1% for Black workers. For White workers, it projects 3.4%, and for Asian workers, 5.8%. The report builds on the McKinsey Global Institute’s “Workforce in motion” study , which found that automation could cut demand for about 36 million U.S. jobs by 2035 while growth elsewhere adds about 41 million. About 11 million workers may need to move into entirely different occupations. Lower-wage workers are 7.6 times as likely as higher-wage workers to be among them. Only about 14% of workers who may need to switch have a direct path into a growing job, meaning minimal retraining and no pay cut. Among workers earning less than $38,000 a year, about 10% do, compared with almost 40% of workers in the top wage bracket. Private AI investment reached nearly $345 billion globally in 2025, according to Stanford’s AI Index, which the report cites. McKinsey finds White workers are 30% to 50% more likely than Black and Latino workers to work in the areas where it expects that capital, and the jobs and wealth that come with it, to concentrate over the next two decades, including AI software, semiconductors, robotics and biotech. The report also points to strain on new workers more broadly. It cites Stanford’s tracking of young workers , which found that employment for 22- to 25-year-olds in some highly AI-exposed jobs is 19% lower than it would be had it kept pace with less-exposed jobs. McKinsey flags risks that could make the gaps worse. About one in six U.S. households has no internet connection, and Black adults are roughly 80% to 90% more likely than White adults to lack broadband. A Stanford study of 4 million job applications cited in the report found that 26% of Black applicants applied to jobs where an AI hiring tool discriminated against their group. The report also argues AI could help at key points in people’s lives. It cites an AI model built on data from Medicaid-enrolled women that flagged pregnancy risks a median of 55 days before standard clinical signs. Simulations projected up to a 31.8% drop in adverse outcomes. On schools, it notes the evidence is mixed and points to New York City’s one-year ban on student-facing AI for pre-K through eighth grade. This is not the first time McKinsey has warned that AI could deepen racial gaps. In 2023, it estimated that generative AI could widen the wealth gap between Black and White households by $43 billion a year by 2045. The new report calls on employers to train frontline workers in AI and hire on skills rather than degrees. It asks investors to require bias testing of AI tools broken out by race, income and geography. It also urges states to use federal broadband funds to reach communities that are still offline. title: Medicare’s hospital fund can pay full benefits only until mid-2033. Next year’s deductible is $1,776
summary: Part A's trust fund can pay full benefits only until the second quarter of 2033. Social Security's retirement fund is projected to run out even sooner, in late 2032.
content: Medicare beneficiaries admitted to the hospital next year will owe $1,776 before Part A coverage starts, up $40 from 2026, the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services announced Nov. 17 . The trust fund that pays for that coverage is running low. Medicare’s Hospital Insurance trust fund can pay full Part A benefits only until the second quarter of 2033, according to the 2026 Social Security and Medicare trustees’ reports , one quarter earlier than last year’s estimate. After that, incoming revenue would cover about 89% of scheduled hospital costs, the Congressional Research Service found. Absent action from Congress, that would mean a roughly 11% cut in what Medicare pays hospitals and other Part A providers. Lawmakers have always stepped in before the fund ran dry, but the deadline is now less than seven years away. Veronique de Rugy, the George Gibbs Chair and a senior research fellow at the Mercatus Center at George Mason University, pressed that point in written testimony for a Nov. 18 Senate Budget Committee hearing on Social Security. She called Medicare “the bigger and faster-growing driver of future debt,” estimating it will add $85 trillion to the national debt by 2056, including interest. What a hospital stay will cost in 2027 Part A covers inpatient hospital care, skilled nursing facility care, hospice and some home health services. The $1,776 deductible covers a beneficiary’s share of the first 60 days of inpatient hospital care in a benefit period, up from $1,736 this year. Longer stays cost more. Patients will owe $444 a day for days 61 through 90, up $10, and $888 a day after that, up $20, while drawing on their lifetime reserve days. Each beneficiary gets 60 lifetime reserve days, and they don’t renew. Once they’re used up, patients pay the full cost of any stay beyond 90 days. The deductible isn’t annual, either. A new benefit period begins after a patient goes 60 consecutive days without inpatient hospital or skilled nursing care, so two hospitalizations months apart can mean paying $1,776 twice. These amounts apply to traditional Medicare. Medicare Advantage plans set their own cost-sharing, and many beneficiaries carry Medigap or other supplemental coverage that covers some or all of these costs. Why the hospital fund is under strain Part A is financed mainly by payroll taxes and the trust fund’s accumulated reserves. Parts B and D, which cover outpatient care and prescription drugs, draw on beneficiary premiums and general Treasury revenue that are reset each year, so they can’t run out of money the same way. Part A spending is projected to exceed the fund’s income starting in 2027, forcing it to draw down reserves. Demand keeps climbing: Medicare covered about 70.7 million people in 2026 at a cost of roughly $1.3 trillion, according to the CRS, with enrollment up 66% since 2005 as baby boomers age into the program. The Medicare Board of Trustees, the group of government officials who monitor the program’s finances, has warned about the hospital fund for years. Its projected depletion date moved up to 2033 from 2036 in last year’s report , and this year the trustees cited higher costs and tax-law changes for pulling it forward another quarter. Social Security’s clock runs out first Social Security’s main retirement fund is in even tighter shape on paper. The trustees project it will be depleted in the fourth quarter of 2032, months before Medicare’s hospital fund, triggering a 22% across-the-board benefit cut unless Congress acts. Social Security’s separate disability fund, by contrast, is projected to stay solvent through at least 2100. De Rugy expects Congress will be tempted to “postpone the reckoning” by shifting money from the disability fund to the retirement fund, a move she argues would buy little time. “A transfer would push the combined depletion date to 2034, a year after Medicare’s hospital fund is expected to run dry,” de Rugy wrote. That would leave lawmakers facing both deadlines within roughly 18 months of each other. The trustees have warned that the closer the hospital fund gets to depletion, the larger the changes needed to fix it will have to be. This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

title: Mike Cannon-Brookes on the string of accidents that created $35 billion Atlassian: ‘Don’t copy our story … It’s not a model for how to do things’
summary: He sent an email to classmates asking if “there's anyone who kind of does not want to get a real job” and whether they wanted to start a new company—with no idea of what that company might be.
content: Today, the enterprise software company Atlassian has a market cap of $35 billion, a revenue run-rate of $8 billion, and 13,000-plus employees worldwide. CEO Mike Cannon-Brookes has a personal net worth of $10 billion, because his ownership of the company was never diluted by VC money when the company was a brand-new startup. But the funny thing about the origins of Atlassian, back in the early 2000s, is that the company formed largely based on a series of accidents, Cannon-Brookes told Fortune . “Don’t copy our story. It’s not very good; it’s not. It’s not a model for how to do things,” he said on a lightning visit to Web Summit in Lisbon. Cannon-Brookes and cofounder Scott Farquhar took the same course at the University of New South Wales. Both had applied only for courses funded by scholarships. Cannon-Brookes originally wanted to be an architect (and jokes that he still would if he ever got the time). But the finances were not there. “Anyone that was going to give you money to go to university, I applied for all sorts of scholarships,” he said. Farquhar had also successfully applied for the Australian Defense Force Academy, but his letter of acceptance got lost in the mail. Thinking he had been rejected, he took one of the same scholarships that Cannon-Brookes had: $15,000 (Australian) per year, tax-free, to do a course that was a mix of computer studies and finance. The course came with a work-experience placement. “We would go to these companies in, like Wisconsin, for six months of installing [Microsoft] Windows” on office desktop computers. This was back in the era when updating operating software meant inserting a physical CD into the machine. “For months, Scott was upgrading Microsoft Windows 95 to Windows 98 or something,” Cannon-Brookes said. “[He] was, like, dude, this is the most boring shit ever. And I had a couple of placements that were similarly mind-numbing.” “The good part about that was, we were both really sour on corporate life.” While he was still an undergrad, Cannon-Brookes had sold a small startup named The Bookmark Box (it helped you manage your bookmarks) to Blink.com , an early web search tool company. With that project done, Cannon-Brookes was at a loose end. He sent an email to some of his classmates asking if “there’s anyone who kind of does not want to get a real job” and whether they wanted to start a new company with him—with no idea of what that company might be—“and Scott was the only person in the three or four that replied.” “And so he’s like, ‘I’m in.’ And so we went ‘Great. We’ll start a business. What should we do?’ Which is the worst way to start a business.” They first planned to work with customer support teams. They grew unhappy with their bug-tracking software, so they built their own. That became Jira, Atlassian’s flagship project and issue tracking tool. Next came the problem of how to sell it. They had a website with a downloadable Word document that customers could fill out with their credit card details, print, and then fax to Atlassian, where Cannon-Brookes and Farquhar would then physically punch the order into their own PC to process the payment. They did this for more than two years. At the time, roughly 2001, the vast majority of software sold over the internet was on DVDs because the internet was delivered on telephone lines, which had extremely limited bandwidth. Cannon-Brookes said that he and his partner had two major hunches early on: “The first hunch was that the internet would be a good way to distribute enterprise software. And the second was that open-source would markedly change the ability for us to make commercial applications at an order of magnitude less price.” “And both turn out to be quite spectacularly correct hunches,” he said. title: Jensen Huang was gone for 11 days. That was Nvidia’s succession test, and the board failed it
summary: A CEO nobody can replace is a CEO nobody can refuse.
content: Jensen Huang’s return to Nvidia is being told as a comeback. The shares jumped about 30% on the news. The founder was back at his desk. Order restored. I read it differently. Those 11 days were the first real test of whether Nvidia could function without the man who built it. The board failed that test, and the way it failed should worry directors at every company whose CEO looks irreplaceable. The sequence of events tells a story. On November 12, Nvidia announced that its board had accepted Huang’s resignation , after reports about his private life and a foreign intelligence operation aimed at him. CFO Colette Kress became interim CEO. The board said it would consider internal and external candidates. Five days later, on the earnings call, chair Harvey Jones told analysts the board did “not intend to reinstate Jensen.” Then the alternatives fell away. The Financial Times reported that the board had approached Rene Haas, the Arm CEO who spent seven years at Nvidia. On November 23, Haas extended his contract at Arm through 2033. The same day, Nvidia’s directors voted unanimously to bring Huang back, saying they had received input from senior levels of the U.S. government . Trump told CNBC that he made a personal assurance that sealed the decision. The board’s own independent investigation is still open. The directors reinstated their CEO before their own inquiry had finished. That’s the detail I can’t get past. A board that says no on a Tuesday and yes six days later has run out of options. A CEO nobody can replace is a CEO nobody can refuse. Accountability depends on a credible alternative. When a board has a successor ready, its questions carry weight, because everyone in the room knows the company survives if the answers fall short. When it has nobody, the CEO holds the leverage and both sides know it. The duty to oversee him turns into a duty to keep him. Huang has run Nvidia since he co-founded it in 1993. The board had three decades to prepare for the day he wasn’t there. When that day came, it had a CFO doing two jobs, one outside name, and a market that wanted him back. Yale’s Jeffrey Sonnenfeld wrote in Fortune the board had no Plan B. Investors made the same point from the other side. Within days of the resignation, prominent shareholders were urging the board to keep the door open to Huang. Nobody outside the company had the facts. What they were pricing was a business with no one else to run it. The board has since created a national security committee and is hiring a chief compliance officer. Those are controls on conduct. Neither one is a successor. I coach CEOs, and I’ve watched how boards arrive here. Nobody decides to skip succession. It gets postponed, one good quarter at a time. Over the years a founder’s identity and the company’s fuse. Raising the question of who comes next starts to feel like disloyalty, so directors leave it for another meeting. The CEO rarely pushes either. Planning your own exit means picturing a company that no longer needs you, and that is the hardest thing to ask of someone whose whole identity is the company. So both sides stay comfortable. The cost arrives on the one day the board needs a choice and finds it doesn’t have one. Plenty of boards are living with the same arrangement right now, and it’s invisible for as long as the results are good. Two tests will tell a director where their board stands. First, name the person who could run the company on Monday. One name, already inside the building, whom the top team would follow. If the honest answer is the CFO as caretaker, you have a holding pattern. Second, recall the last time the board said no to the CEO on something he cared about. If nobody can remember one, the board has already stopped overseeing him. It just hasn’t been tested yet. Huang may prove to be the right leader for Nvidia’s next chapter. The investigation may answer every open question. Neither would change what the 11 days showed. The board now enters the next crisis in a weaker position than the last one. It has shown its investors, its government and its CEO that it has no alternative to him. He knows it. So does everyone who will ever need to challenge him. Every director reading this should ask the question Nvidia’s board had to answer in public. If our CEO were gone tomorrow, would we have a choice? title: Shoppers helped pay Trump’s tariffs. Now Target, Best Buy, and Kohl’s are booking $387 million in refunds
summary: The three retailers booked $387 million in refund benefits last quarter, while Walmart and Target say they're cutting prices rather than paying shoppers back.
content: American consumers helped foot the bill for President Donald Trump’s tariffs as retailers passed higher import costs on through price increases. Now the refunds are flowing back, and they are showing up in retailers’ profits rather than in shoppers’ bank accounts. Best Buy and Kohl’s both reported better-than-expected quarterly results on Tuesday, after Target beat expectations last week. Together, the three retailers recognized $387 million in tariff refund benefits in their latest quarters. The money traces back to February, when the Supreme Court ruled that the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA) did not authorize the president to impose tariffs, invalidating a significant portion of Trump’s tariff regime. As of Nov. 5, U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) had certified approximately $128.4 billion in tariff refunds, including interest, and sent them to the Treasury Department for payment, according to a Nov. 10 filing with the U.S. Court of International Trade. Tariff refunds are boosting retailers’ profits Kohl’s reported third-quarter comparable sales growth of just 1.2%, yet its net income jumped to $254 million from $8 million a year earlier. Much of that came from one-time items: a $137 million tax benefit, a $61 million gain from the sale of two properties, and $45 million in tariff refund benefits, according to the company’s third-quarter earnings release . The department store chain has received approximately $190 million in tariff refunds this fiscal year. It now expects those refunds to add $1.03 to its full-year earnings per share, nearly a quarter of its raised forecast of $4.30 to $4.50. Best Buy reported comparable sales growth of 6.1%, its strongest in five years, in Jason Bonfig’s first earnings report as CEO . Net income more than doubled to $353 million from $140 million, according to the company’s earnings release . In May 2025, Best Buy’s then-CEO Corie Barry said the electronics retailer had already raised prices on some products to offset the costs of Trump’s tariffs. This quarter, the company recorded $41 million in tariff refund benefits, which helped lift profitability. Target has recognized approximately $1.3 billion in tariff refund benefits in the first nine months of its fiscal year, including $301 million in the third quarter alone. Its quarterly net income rose to $1.2 billion from $689 million, and tariff refunds accounted for $228 million of that after taxes, or nearly a fifth, according to Target’s third-quarter results . All three retailers are seeing sales rebound. But the refunds are boosting profits without requiring them to sell a single extra product. Shoppers paid a large share of the tariffs Best Buy was far from alone in passing higher import costs on to shoppers. An April analysis by Harvard Business School researchers , who tracked daily prices of nearly 360,000 products at five major U.S. retailers, estimated that consumers shouldered up to 43% of the tariff costs in the first seven months after the new tariffs were imposed. U.S. businesses absorbed the rest. Trump’s tariffs amounted to an average tax increase of $1,000 per U.S. household in 2025, according to estimates from the Tax Foundation . In February, Goldman Sachs economists estimated that tariffs had raised core PCE prices, the Federal Reserve’s preferred inflation gauge, by about 0.7% through January. The effect outlasted the ruling. Researchers at the Federal Reserve Bank of New York and Columbia University estimated that consumer goods prices were still about 2% higher in August than they would have been without the tariffs imposed since early 2025. Some Americans who paid customs charges directly on overseas purchases are receiving refunds through shipping companies including FedEx , UPS , and DHL . The federal refund system offers no such relief to shoppers who paid higher prices at their local stores. Lawmakers are pressing companies to give the money back Earlier this month, Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) and fellow Democratic senators asked the Federal Trade Commission to investigate whether companies that raised prices in response to tariffs and then kept the refunds violated federal law. Warren’s office accused corporations of “pocketing tariff refunds after raising prices on consumers.” The senators cited responses from five major companies: Walmart , Nike , Apple , Target, and Energizer. None committed to directly reimbursing consumers who had paid higher prices because of the tariffs. Several major companies have either ruled out direct refunds to shoppers or remained silent on the issue, as Fortune previously reported . In August, Walmart said it was using its tariff refunds to lower prices, having received nearly all of the $2.9 billion it was owed. CBS News reported that the retailer cut prices on thousands of items in July. Target is doing the same. In August, Target CFO Jim Lee said the retailer would focus on lowering prices but made no commitment to directly refunding shoppers. The retailer said last week it had lowered prices on nearly 2,000 home, apparel, and accessories products during the third quarter, on top of more than 10,000 price reductions over the past year. But lowering prices for future purchases is different from compensating customers for past ones. A shopper who paid more for a television or a piece of furniture last year may have no reason to buy another one this holiday season, even if it is now cheaper. title: Trump has found something to blame for his midterm loss: ‘Fake’ growth numbers out of Howard Lutnick’s Commerce Department
summary: "This is not a small error, this is a massive, and purposeful, error," Trump wrote on Truth Social.
content: The headaches just keep piling up for Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has been on his case about the Commerce Department’s handling of Nvidia , following the news of Jensen Huang’s affair with an alleged Chinese spy. And now President Trump is blaming his team for publishing “fake” growth numbers before the midterms. “It was just revealed that the real numbers on the economy, published before the election, were fake, and a correction was issued yesterday by the people in the government agency that does these numbers,” the president posted on Truth Social . “The American economy under the Trump administration is doing far better than the good numbers already released.” The agency Trump appears to be referring to is the Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA), which sits within the Commerce Department. The BEA operates with statistical and methodological independence, a safeguard designed to protect the accuracy and impartiality of its statistics. On Wednesday, the BEA issued revisions to its growth figures for the third quarter of 2026, saying GDP was 4.3%—not the 3.9% it had originally forecast. The upward revision of 0.9% on the initial estimate was “primarily reflecting upward revisions to investment and consumer spending.” Analysts are unlikely to be surprised. Revisions are a routine feature of U.S. economic statistics. Lower survey response rates have reduced the precision of some estimates. As UBS’s Pauk Donovan said in a note to clients this morning: “Changes in U.S. economic growth are exaggerated by the fiction of annualization (a technique employed by very few advanced economies).” “Data revisions are more common as structural change and poor survey response rates reduce precision.” But President Trump suggested there were more nefarious reasons for the near-percentage-point difference in initial estimates to the published figures: “Why wasn’t the correct number issued before the election? I am asking for an immediate investigation of this situation. This is not a small error, this is a massive, and purposeful, error.” Lutnick issued a bullish economic update. Writing on X, the Commerce Secretary said: “We’re bringing American manufacturing back at a scale nobody thought possible. America’s successes will become even more powerful in the coming years as these projects move from groundbreaking to full production.” Trusting U.S. data Trump’s latest clash with federal data agencies could further undermine confidence in U.S. economic statistics. In 2025, the president fired the director of the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS), Erika McEntarfer, claiming she had overseen the publishing of “phony” job numbers for political reasons. (The president provided no evidence for his claim.) This, paired with Trump’s extraordinary attacks on the Federal Reserve under former chairman Jerome Powell, led many economists and investors to worry about the credibility of major U.S. institutions that either inform policy or make it. At the time, Alberto Cavallo, Professor at Harvard Business School, told Goldman Sachs : “It’s difficult to avoid a comparison to the experience of my home country, Argentina, nearly two decades ago when the president, dismayed at rising inflation, removed statistical agency leadership. “Some statistics stopped being reported, and official data no longer seemed to align with perceptions. That was a very chaotic period that destroyed trust in Argentina’s official statistics for over a decade.” While Cavallo said the U.S. is ahead of some of Argentina’s data bodies in terms of skills and institutional checks and balances, he said the situation was still “very concerning.” This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

title: In 2026, many employers are ditching merit-based pay bumps in favor of ‘peanut butter raises’
summary: Bucking the trend of rewarding only top staffers, around 44% of companies are planning fixed pay bumps spread out evenly to all their employees—and it could help low-income workers.
content: Professionals have long been taught a simple formula for career success: work hard, outperform your peers, and bigger paychecks will follow. But this year, employers are planning to reward their star staffers differently; instead of factoring in merit, more companies are considering general pay hikes spread out evenly, dubbed the “peanut butter raises” trend. Around 44% of employers plan to roll out uniform, across-the-board wage bumps in 2026, according to a 2026 Payscale report . About 16% of organizations are newly implementing these “peanut butter” raises: 9% say they already employ the pay strategy, and another 18% of organizations are considering it this year. And top-performing companies are all-in on the approach. Around 56% of organizations that reported that they would exceed their revenue goals in 2025 are using or actively considering peanut butter pay increases. Companies are still planning to boost employee pay by 3.5%, the same rate as last year. And while 48% of businesses will continue the tradition of awarding pay bumps based on worker performance—which the report described as a “best practice”—the new compensation fad may be trying to alleviate financial headwinds for low-paid workers. “Tying merit pay increases to performance ratings has come under criticism in recent years for being too subjective and prone to bias,” the Payscale report noted. “At the same time, some organizations have made headlines by electing to standardize pay increases to alleviate administrative burden and reward workers equally, especially for low wage workers where inflation is a big concern.” Dwindling pay budgets and flat raises amid economic uncertainty Job seekers and staffers alike are suffering through a difficult labor market: Hiring has slowed, layoffs are steadily streaming in, and wages don’t feel like they’re holding up. Looking at the year ahead, the picture doesn’t look too pretty. Wall Street analysts and business executives have been floating the idea we’re in a “ K-shaped economy ”; higher-income Americans are witnessing their earnings and wealth rise, while lower-income people are struggling against smaller gains and the high cost of living. The concept has come to explain the confusing U.S. economy, where solid overall growth contrasts with sluggish hiring and rising unemployment. While U.S. companies are holding their average salary increase budget steady at 3.5%, according to a 2025 report from Willis Towers Watson , there’s a large cohort that is planning to scale back. Nearly a third of businesses plan to lower their compensation -increase budgets compared to last year, citing a potential recession, dwindling financial performance, and desire for more control over costs. Last year, one high-profile employer ditched its merit-based raises in favor of a general, flat pay bump. Starbucks announced it would be giving a standard 2% raise to all salaried North American employees in 2025, diverging from the norm that managers have a say in the raises of their direct reports. It was all a part of CEO Brian Niccol’s bid to reduce costs in a broader company turnaround effort. But Starbucks is just one notable name in a growing list of employers hunkering down for economic hardship. Lexi Clarke, Payscale’s chief people officer, told Fortune last year that pay-increase budgets are being slimmed as tariffs and economic woes create uncertainty, forcing many employers to be on their guard. “Economic concerns have now overtaken labor competition as the primary driver of compensation decisions,” Clarke said , as “66% of employers cite this as the reason for pulling back, up 17% from last year.” As more companies trim back wage budgets and hand out peanut butter raises, there are many still reinvesting in their star talent. America’s largest private employer, $988 billion retail titan Walmart , unrolled a strategy in 2024 to pay its top store managers up to $620,000 per year. U.S. CEO John Furner said it was a way to “make managers feel like owners,” acknowledging their success with a slice of the profit pie. Their average base pay was hiked from $130,000 to $160,000, raising their total compensation to between $420,000 and $620,000 annually. And with more than 4,000 store managers across the U.S. (and around 1.5 million workers) when the policy went into effect, the payout wasn’t just generous—it was a calculated bet on culture.
